title: Why online lessons are intense and her new note-card system
summary: She and Rowe discuss the drain of online teaching and the loss of the social side; she organizes files and books for each student.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I noticed, I did a little bit of it to finish the Hamilton semester, and I also experienced that sort of intensity — I’m not sure what it comes from but it does sort of drain you.

Well for me, part of it is, you know, I mean just the physical presence of the kids is so delightful. And they do these funny things, you know, they pull the wrinkles on my arm, or crazy stuff. And the parent brings me a cup of coffee. You know it really makes it a lot more anecdotal.
You’re taking the social element out of it.
And it get to say hello to the dogs, all the dogs are my friends.
Oh I hadn’t thought of that. So it’s not so much what it adds on it’s what it takes away I guess.

Well yeah I mean there’s both you know. But that’s I think what makes it so intense is that it’s really — so now I have a system. I have a beautiful big folder, you know, with note cards for every kid. Every lesson I take notes, I know exactly where I am. I have my books all organized so I know which books to pull out. I don’t normally have to do that. And that makes it a lot easier. So every day I pull out my huge notebook, it’s a 3-ring. And then I pull out the files for the kids I’m going to teach that day and then I pull out those books and I look over my notes and I practice those instruments and then I’m all ready.
